meta_description: How to tell a healthy aroid root from a rotting one, when to chop, when to wait, and the cheap pothos test most growers skip.
title: Reading Aroid Roots
deck: A field guide to the white, the tan, the mush, and the cheap pothos that will tell you whether your substrate is lying to you.
intro: The first time I cut open a _Philodendron gloriosum_ that had been sulking for three months, the rhizome looked like a wet cigar. The outer cortex slipped off in my fingers like a sock. Underneath, where there should have been firm, pale tissue the color of a peeled almond, there was a brown stripe running the length of the stem. I had been watering on a schedule. I had been misting. I had been, in every visible sense, a responsible adult.

Roots tell the truth that leaves are too polite to mention. By the time a velvet philodendron throws a yellow lower leaf or an anthurium puts out a runt with crisped margins, the conversation underground has been going on for weeks. Learning to read what is happening below the line — without uprooting the plant every Sunday like an anxious dentist — is the single skill that separates collectors who lose a _spiritus-sancti_ from collectors who keep one alive for a decade.
pull_quote: Roots tell the truth that leaves are too polite to mention; by the time a leaf yellows, the conversation underground is weeks old.

sections.heading: What a healthy aroid root actually looks like
paragraphs: Forget the stock-photo version. A healthy aroid root is not blinding white. The growing tip — the last inch or two — is white to cream, sometimes faintly green where light hits it, and firm enough to bend without snapping. The older tissue behind that tip will tan with age. A two-year-old _Monstera deliciosa_ root the diameter of a pencil can be the color of weak tea and still be perfectly alive. Color alone is a bad diagnostic.

Texture is the better tell. Healthy roots are turgid. Press one gently between thumb and forefinger and it should feel like a piece of cooked spaghetti that's still got bite — yielding but resistant, with a sheath that stays put. The cortex, that outer layer, should not slide off. If you can pull the root through your pinched fingers and strip it like a wire, leaving a thin string of vascular tissue behind, that root is dead. The string itself — the stele — may still be intact and pale, which is why some growers convince themselves the plant is fine. It isn't. A stripped root is a wick, not a pump.

Smell the rootball. This sounds absurd until you do it once. Living aroid roots in a well-aerated mix smell like wet bark and faint mushroom, clean and a little sweet. Roots in trouble smell sour, swampy, or — at the far end — like a forgotten vase of cut flowers. If you open a pot and step back from the smell, you already have your answer.

sections.heading: The four stages of rot, and which ones are reversible
paragraphs: Rot is not a single event. It is a sequence, and where you intervene determines whether you keep the plant, the growth point, or nothing. Stage one is **suffocation** — roots browning at the tips because the substrate has compacted or stayed saturated. The tissue is still firm. Repot into something airier and most plants shrug it off in a month.

Stage two is **soft rot of the fine roots** while the main structural roots and stem remain firm. You'll find black, slimy threads in the bottom third of the pot. This is recoverable: trim to clean tissue, wash the remaining roots under tepid water, and re-pot into pure perlite or a chunky bark-perlite blend until new roots establish. Skip fertilizer for three weeks. A humidity-stable spot helps; a sealed bin is overkill for most genera and invites a new problem.

Stage three is **stem rot creeping into the rhizome or caudex**. Now you are doing surgery. Cut above any brown vascular streaking — that thin internal stripe is the rot's road map — until the cross-section is uniformly pale. Dust with cinnamon or a sulfur-based fungicide if you like rituals; the cleaner cut matters more than the powder. Stage four is when the growth point itself is mush. At that point you are not saving the plant. You are, at best, salvaging a node further up the stem that hasn't been reached yet, and even then the odds are not in your favor.

sections.heading: When to chop, when to wait
paragraphs: The instinct of a new collector is to chop at the first sign of trouble. The instinct of an experienced one is to wait, because chopping a plant that didn't need it costs you a year of growth and sometimes the lead growth point entirely. The question to ask is not 'are the roots damaged' but 'is the damage advancing'.

Wait if the plant has a firm stem, at least one healthy leaf, and root damage confined to the fine feeders. Repot, correct the underlying cause — usually substrate, sometimes watering cadence, occasionally a cold draft from a winter window — and give it six weeks. _Anthurium_ in particular will often look catatonic for a month and then push a cataphyll out of nowhere. They do not want to be disturbed twice.

Chop without hesitation when you see brown vascular streaking inside the stem on a cut, when the base of the petioles is going translucent, or when a previously firm caudex on a _Philodendron verrucosum_ or _luxurians_ has gone spongy. Cut above the damage, cut clean with a blade you flamed or wiped with isopropyl, and root the top in sphagnum or perlite. A chop made on Tuesday beats a chop made the following Tuesday by a wide margin; rot moves in millimeters per day in warm conditions.

sections.heading: The pothos test no one teaches you
paragraphs: Here is the trick that should be in every care guide and isn't. Buy a cheap golden pothos. Pot it in exactly the same substrate, in an identical pot, sitting next to your rare plant. Water both on the same schedule. The pothos is your canary.

Pothos roots aggressively in almost any condition that isn't actively hostile. If your _Anthurium warocqueanum_ is declining and the pothos beside it is also stalling — yellowing lower leaves, no new growth, roots browning — the problem is environmental: your mix is staying too wet, your tap water is too hard, your room is too cold at night, your light is weaker than your meter suggests. If the pothos is throwing a new leaf every two weeks and the _warocqueanum_ is sulking, the problem is specific to the queen: she wants more humidity, finer media around the root initials, or simply more time.

This sounds like a parlor trick. It is actually the cheapest diagnostic instrument in the hobby. A four-dollar pothos will tell you, over six weeks, things a moisture meter and a hygrometer cannot, because it integrates every variable in your room into a single living readout. I keep one on every shelf. They are not decorative. They are instruments.

sections.heading: Substrate is a root question, not a recipe
paragraphs: Most rot starts with substrate, and most substrate advice online is given as a recipe — two parts bark, one part perlite, one part charcoal, a handful of worm castings — as if the components mattered more than the behavior. They don't. What matters is how the mix behaves wet and how fast it dries in your specific conditions.

Squeeze a handful of your mix after watering. Water should come out in drops, not a stream, and the mix should spring back open when you release it. A day later, the surface should look dry and the core should still feel cool and barely damp. If the core is wet three days in, your mix is too fine or your pot is too large. If the whole thing is bone dry in 36 hours, you'll be chasing dehydration and salt buildup all summer.

Aroid roots want air at least as much as they want water. The wild epiphytes — most _Anthurium_, climbing _Philodendron_, _Rhaphidophora_ — evolved clinging to bark with roots half-exposed to moving air. Replicate that and rot becomes rare. Bury those same roots in dense peat and you are running an experiment in anaerobic bacteria. The plant will tell you which one you chose, eventually, through the leaves. But the roots knew first.

sections.heading: Reading the pot without unpotting
paragraphs: You should not be pulling your plants out every month. It damages the fine root hairs that do most of the actual work and stresses species — _gloriosum_, _plowmanii_, mature _Anthurium clarinervium_ — that resent any disturbance. Learn to read the pot from the outside.

Lift it. Weight is the most honest sensor you own. A pot that feels heavy four days after watering, when a healthy plant of that size should be approaching dry, is holding water it shouldn't. Look at the drainage holes: white root tips poking through are a good sign, brown stubs are not. Check the soil line. A surface that has sunk significantly means the organic fraction has broken down and the mix is collapsing — time to repot before the roots suffocate.

Smell the drainage tray after a watering. Clean water smells like nothing. Water that smells faintly of pond is carrying decomposition products out of the pot, and that's your warning shot. If you take only one habit from this essay, take that one: water, wait ten minutes, sniff the runoff. Your nose will catch a problem two weeks before your eyes will.
